query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In HEA nanoparticles, a well-ordered (SRO‐rich) interior retards melting; however, when surface segregation (e.g., oxidation or elemental enrichment) occurs at the nanoparticle exterior, it disrupts the energetic stability imposed by SRO, thereby lowering the onset temperature of premelting.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HEA nanoparticles (e.g., CoFeNiCr or CoFeNiMn) synthesized to exhibit significant interior short-range order.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled post‐synthesis treatment that either promotes surface segregation (e.g., mild annealing in air) or preserves a clean, minimally oxidized surface (e.g., annealing in an inert atmosphere such as high-purity argon).
generation.conditions: Nanoparticles with diameters below ~10 nm, subjected to incremental in situ TEM heating from room temperature up to melting, under catalysis-relevant conditions (i.e., similar to operating temperatures for catalytic or energy applications).
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of surface composition alteration (e.g., oxidation or elemental enrichment at the nanoparticle surface) relative to the SRO-dominated core.
generation.mechanism: The internally ordered (SRO) regions of HEA nanoparticles provide enhanced energetic stability by reducing the free energy slope with temperature; however, if surface segregation or oxidation occurs, it creates a destabilized outer layer with a reduced energy barrier to atomic displacements. This surface layer thus acts as a nucleation site for premelting, effectively lowering the overall temperature at which premelting initiates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that experience surface segregation (via air annealing) will display a lower onset of premelting and a broader, less sharp melting transition compared to nanoparticles processed under inert conditions that maintain minimal surface modifications. This effect should be more pronounced for particles below ~10 nm.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles post-treated in an inert atmosphere, with preserved surface stoichiometry and strong interior SRO, exhibiting higher premelting temperatures and sharper melting transitions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for equiatomic, SRO-rich HEA nanoparticles (both FCC and BCC structured) in the sub-10 nm size range. It may not be observed in systems with weak or no SRO, in significantly larger nanoparticles where surface-to-volume ratio effects are negligible, or under conditions with extreme surface reconstruction not typical of catalysis-relevant treatments.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal integrates evidence on SRO enhancing thermal stability (PMC11265590::web::022::sro_effect_on_thermal_stability) and size-dependent melting behavior (PMC6479918::web::000::abstract), and extends ideas of surface segregation effects observed in laser-generated nanoparticles (PMC9064730::web::012::crystal_structure_of_the_laser_generated). The new aspect is the explicit mechanistic linking of surface segregation to the disruption of SRO stabilization, whose quantitative impact on premelting onset remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with identical bulk compositions and SRO but differing only in the degree of surface modification. One set is post-treated in air to induce surface segregation/oxidation, and the other is annealed in an inert atmosphere to preserve clean surfaces. Perform controlled in situ TEM heating experiments with simultaneous surface chemical analysis (e.g., EELS or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to track both the onset of premelting (via morphological and diffraction changes) and surface composition changes.
measurements: Premelting onset temperature (identified as the temperature at which surface disorder or partial melting is first observed)
Melting transition sharpness (width of transition temperature range)
Surface chemical composition before and after heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the air-treated nanoparticles (with promoted surface segregation) do not exhibit a significantly lower premelting onset or broader melting transition compared to the inert-treated nanoparticles—and if their surface composition does not correlate with the melting behavior—then the hypothesized mechanistic role of surface segregation in disrupting SRO stabilization is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To understand the elemental behavior in the thermal stability, Ghosh et al. discovered a first-order order–disorder transition from a high-temperature random structure to an ordered one occurring at approximately 975 K in the CrCoNi HEA utilizing on-lattice machine learning interatomic potentials and canonical Monte Carlo (MC) simulations. Moreover, different degrees of chemical SRO in the nanoscratching process have been examined by hybrid MC/molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, revealing that the SRO-600K sample displayed enhanced resistance to plastic deformation and increased structural stability. As a result, the issue of the chemical SRO effect has attracted growing interest in the past 20 years within the community,e.g., studies on the thermal stability of local chemical ordering and its impact on the mechanical properties of HEAs.

The thermal stability of the Cr-rich Cr54 HEA is comparatively worse, and according to the correlations between the change in Gibbs free energy and temperature, a phase transition in this alloy system occurs at T = 883 K. Comparing the SQS and SRO structures of the CoFeNiCr HEA, it is observed that the thermal stability of the structure after MC iterations is better than that of the initial random structure. This suggests that chemical ordering contributes to the enhancement of the thermal stability of HEAs. In the case of the CoFeNiMn HEA, lacking chemical ordering, the correlations between the change in Gibbs free energy and temperature in the structures before and after MC iterations are relatively close. AbstractUsing the molecular dynamics method, the melting character, mechanical properties, microstructures, and strain deformation mechanisms of nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy are systematically investigated in the present work. The simulation results suggest that the melting point in CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy decreases with the grain size, decreasing from 3.6 to 2.0 nm. The grain size has a significant effect on shear and Young’s modulus compared to bulk modulus. The stress-strain simulation demonstrates that the ultimate tensile strength decreases with the decrease of the grain size, while the plastic deformation increases with the decrease in grain size. While the average grain size decreases to 2.0 nm, the amorphization induced by small grain size reduces plastic deformation. The common neighbor analysis shows that the face-centered cubic (FCC) composition of CoCrFeNiMn decreases gradually with decreasing grain size. For the sample with a grain size of 2.0 nm, the FCC composition is about 19% at a strain of 20%, accompanied by severe amorphization. cited_evidence.text: The size selectivity of the surface segregation of Cr and Mn, which probably occurred along with the oxidation in the spinel structure, indicated an origin in the formation of the NPs. This finding agreed with the results of the atomistic model on the formation of NPs in the ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of metals in liquids. The results of the model predict different residence times of larger NPs released from the molten surface layer into the hot, low-density mixing region of the ablated metal species and the supercritical solvent according to their kinetic energies. The movements of the laser-ablated species away from the ablation target at different velocities was also shown experimentally for the femtosecond-pulsed laser ablation of aluminum in vacuum. A longer residence time in the low-density mixing region probably caused an intensified interaction with oxygen, which formed during the splitting of the solvent. Subsequently, the surface segregation of Cr and Mn took place by selective oxidation in our experiments. Both metals naturally exhibit a higher oxidation potential than Co, Fe and Ni.
